transcription.tex: Is ‘tangent’ (\(\tan \)) in trigonometry related to the ‘tangent’ of a circle?

A tangent is a trigonometric function (which inputs an angle and gives you the ratio between the opposite and adjacent sides of a right-angled triangle), but also a line which touches a circle. Are they related?
Just as ‘radius’ can refer either to the line itself or its length, we have names for other special lines, which can also refer to their lengths:
A common myth is that \(\sin \), \(\cos \) and \(\tan \) are the ‘core’ trigonometric functions.
A tangent is a line which touches the circle. We’re interested in the length just between the touching point and where it meets the secant.
Sine (sort of) comes from the word for ‘bowstring’. It refers to half the line if we doubled up the arc and connected the two ends.
A secant (shortened to ‘sec’) is a line which cuts the circle. In a trig setting, we’re interested in the length from the circle centre to where it meets the tangent.

transcription.tex:
Suppose we let the radius of the sector be 1. Then if we define \(\sin  \theta =\frac{opp}{hyp}\) and \(\tan  \theta =\frac{opp}{adj}\) and \(\sec  \theta =\frac{hyp}{adj}\) then this conveniently gives us:\par \(\sin  \theta =\frac{a}{1}=a\hspace{2.52em}\tan  \theta =\frac{b}{1}=b\)
\(\sec  \theta =\frac{c}{1}=c\)\par i.e. \(\sin  \theta \), \(\tan  \theta \) and \(\sec  \theta \) actually give us the lengths of the sine, tangent and secant respectively.
And hence \(\tan  \theta \) and the length of the ‘tangent’ are clearly linked!
“So if \(\sin \), \(\tan \) and \(\sec \) are the ‘core’ trigonometric functions, where does \({{c}{o}{s}}\) come into the fray?”

“cosine” (\(\cos \)), “cotangent” (\(\cot \)) and “cosecant” (\(\operatorname{cosec}\)) are the ‘complementary’ trig functions. Complementary angles add to \(90^{\circ}\).\par The two smaller angles in a right-angled triangle are clearly complementary.

The complementary sine (cosine) of an angle is by definition the sine of the complementary angle, e.g. \(\cos  \left(40^{\circ}\right)=\sin  \left(50^{\circ}\right)\). Thus:\par \(\cos  \left(\theta \right)=\sin  \left(90^{\circ}-\theta \right)\hspace{1.12em}\operatorname{cosec} \left(\theta \right)=\sec  \left(90^{\circ}-\theta \right)\hspace{0.56em}\)
\(\mathrm{co}t \left(\theta \right)=\tan  \left(90^{\circ}-\theta \right)\)

The complementary definition gives \(\cot\theta=\tan(\pi/2-\theta)=\cos\theta/\sin\theta\). Interchanging opposite and adjacent leads to \(1/\tan\theta\) wherever that reciprocal is defined. The quotient \(\cos\theta/\sin\theta\) also defines cotangent where \(\cos\theta=0\).

transcription.tex: 6. Given \(\arcsin x=k\), \(0<k<\pi/2\):\par a. State the possible values of \(x\).\par b. Express i. \(\cos k\), ii. \(\tan k\), in terms of \(x\).\par c. How do the answers to b change if \(-\pi/2<k<0\)?
a. \(x=\sin k\). Sine is increasing on the principal interval, so \(0<\sin k<\sin(\pi/2)\), hence \(0<x<1\).
b(i). \(\cos k=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2k}=\pm\sqrt{1-x^2}\). Since \(k\) is in quadrant 1, \(\cos k>0\):\[\cos k=\sqrt{1-x^2}.\]
c. \(k\) is now in quadrant 4. Cosine remains positive, so the formula for \(\cos k\) is unchanged. Tangent changes sign because \(x<0\); its formula is unchanged.
